title: Picking up snacks at a dépanneur in Montréal
setting: It's a snowy afternoon in Montréal's Plateau neighbourhood. You pop into the "dép" — the dépanneur, or corner store — on your street to grab a drink and some chips before meeting friends.
objectives: Finish a purchase in Québec French
Understand why the price at the till is higher than on the shelf
Recognise everyday Québec expressions like "C'est beau" and "Bienvenue"
varietyNote: This is Québec French as heard in Montréal. It has its own accent, vocabulary and expressions, and some words mean something different than in France — "bienvenue", for example. French from France is understood here too, and Québécois French varies across the province.

phrases.translation: Hello! (in French and English at once)
phrases.exampleTranslation: Answering in French keeps the conversation in French.
phrases.note: A Montréal greeting that lets you choose the language. Answer "Bonjour !" to continue in French.

phrases.example: Je vais au dép chercher du lait.
phrases.exampleTranslation: I'm going to the corner store to get some milk.
phrases.note: A Québec word. In France you'd say "l'épicerie" or "la supérette".

phrases.example: —Ce sera tout ? —Oui, ce sera tout, merci.
phrases.exampleTranslation: "Will that be all?" "Yes, that'll be all, thanks."

phrases.example: —Désolé pour l'attente ! —C'est beau, pas de problème.
phrases.exampleTranslation: "Sorry for the wait!" "It's all good, no problem."
phrases.note: In Québec, "c'est beau" often means "it's fine" or "we're done" — not only "it's beautiful".

alsoHeard.where: Also very common in Québec for "it's fine / OK"

phrases.note: In France, "bienvenue" only means "welcome (to a place)". In Québec it's also the everyday reply to "merci".

phrases.translation: Have a good rest of your day!
phrases.exampleTranslation: Thanks, have a good rest of your day!

cultureNotes: Montréal is bilingual in practice. "Bonjour-hi" invites you to choose; answering in French usually keeps things in French — and saying you're practising your French is always welcome.
Prices on the shelf usually don't include sales tax in Canada. Tax is added at the till, so the total is higher than the sticker price.
People in Québec often switch to "tu" (informal you) faster than in France, especially with younger people.
Dépanneurs are neighbourhood staples — snacks, drinks, milk, and often beer and wine.

steps.text: You shake the snow off your boots as you walk in. The cashier looks up from his phone.

steps.prompt: What does "Bonjour-hi" mean, and how should you answer if you want to practise your French?

options.text: It's a bilingual greeting — answer "Bonjour !" to continue in French.
options.why: Exactly. He's letting you choose the language, and "Bonjour !" keeps it in French.

options.text: It means "Goodbye" — he's closing the store.
options.why: It's a hello, combining French "bonjour" and English "hi".

options.text: It's a joke — you should laugh and answer in English.
options.why: It's a normal Montréal greeting, not a joke. You can answer in either language.

steps.text: You bring a bottle of juice and a bag of chips to the counter.

steps.prompt: That's everything. How do you answer?

options.why: Polite and natural — the same phrase works in Québec and France.
"C'est fini" means "it's over", which sounds strange here.
He asked "Will that be all?" — answering "No" tells him you want something else.

steps.text: You're surprised — the shelf labels added up to $5.99.

steps.prompt: Why is the total higher than the shelf prices?

options.text: Sales tax is added at the till — shelf prices in Canada usually don't include it.
options.why: Right. Tax is added when you pay, so expect totals to be a little higher.

options.text: The cashier made a mistake — you should complain.
options.why: It's not a mistake. Canadian shelf prices normally exclude sales tax.

options.text: There's an extra charge for paying by card.
options.why: Card payments don't usually cost extra. The difference is sales tax.

steps.speaker: Cashier
steps.text: Désolé, la machine est lente aujourd'hui… OK, c'est beau !
steps.translation: Sorry, the machine is slow today… OK, all set!

options.text: All set / It's all good — the payment went through
options.why: In Québec, "c'est beau" often means "it's fine" or "we're done".
That's the literal meaning, but here he's telling you the payment worked.
"Beau" has nothing to do with price here. It means everything is fine.

steps.text: You pick up your things and say "Merci !"

steps.speaker: Cashier
steps.translation: You're welcome! Have a good rest of your day!

steps.prompt: Why does the cashier say "Bienvenue" as you leave?

options.text: In Québec, "bienvenue" is a normal way to say "you're welcome" after "merci".
options.why: Right. In France you'd hear "de rien" instead — but in Québec, "bienvenue" is everyday.

options.text: He's welcoming you to the store — he didn't notice you've been there a while.
options.why: "Bienvenue" can mean "welcome (to a place)", but here it answers your "merci".

options.text: He's inviting you to come back tomorrow.
options.why: It's simply "you're welcome". "Bonne fin de journée" is the goodbye.
